Alex.note: As the Eagle I visit one player and learn their visitors, gaining one egg per visitor. I'll visit Finley, who has been quiet and is a fresh read this round.

Blair.note: I'm Farm as the Hawk again, and I'm behind on points. I'll visit Ellis to check for Meowfia, since a Hawk visit pays an egg only on a Meowfia target.

Drew.note: I'm Farm with the Falcon and need a big round to catch Casey. Ellis threw two cards at me last round, so I'll visit Ellis to see who they visited.

Ellis.note: As the Floofer I hug my target so their night role does nothing. Blair has been pressing hard, so hugging Blair blocks their Hawk role tonight.

Finley.note: As the Kookaburra I learn a player's role. Blair's Hawk claim is the most checkable, so I'll visit Blair.

events.text: Finley was visited by: nobody else.

audit: Blair (Hawk) is hugged: no effect at tier 50
Drew (Falcon) is hugged: no effect at tier 60

Alex.feeling: Messy round: two Falcon claims, Ellis switched roles under pressure, and Finley's unexplained -2 keeps the table guessing, so I'm fairly confident about Ellis but not sure.

Blair.feeling: Tense and muddled: the claims conflict, Drew's Falcon story looks like a lie, and the table is closing in on Ellis, whom my Hawk visit cleared.

Casey.feeling: Messy and contradictory: Ellis keeps switching roles, but Finley's nest loss and the mixed Falcon and Hawk stories leave me less sure than I'd like.

Drew.feeling: Tense and muddled: Ellis's shifting Falcon and Owl claims give us a real lead, but the confused reports and Finley's -2 make the other reads shaky.

Ellis.feeling: I'm Meowfia this round and the table is closing in on me, so this feels tense and exposed.

Finley.feeling: Round 3 is messy: my confused Kookaburra report makes my own information unreliable, and Ellis's role switch is the clearest lead on the table.

Alex.note: Ellis is my target. I'll throw my D2, a low card, one vote is enough to add to the pile at Ellis without risking my high cards.

Blair.note: Ellis is Farm by my Hawk check, so I want the lynch to fall on someone else. Drew's Falcon claim is the contradiction, so I'll throw three low cards at Drew.

Casey.note: Ellis is the lean after switching roles. I'll throw my low cards H5 and W7 at Ellis to add votes while keeping my high cards.

Drew.note: Ellis is the likeliest Meowfia after the role switch. I'll throw two cards at Ellis, the Wild W4 and the 3, to add votes while banking a little value if Farm wins.

Ellis.note: I'm Meowfia and the table has seven votes-worth against me, so I'll likely be eggsecuted. I'll throw only my Wild at Drew to keep my high cards; if my side loses, my best card returns to my nest.

Finley.note: Same plan: throw S7 at Ellis, the strongest suspect after the role switch.

Alex.confusing: The Kookaburra's confusion was hard to track, since a confused player's report is wrong but they still draw or discard as told. Nests moving without a clear source made the day harder to read.
Alex.fun: Round 1 was fun: the Mouser claim about Ellis's Turkey looked suspicious until the Turkey correction explained Blair's +1, and the table turned on Blair.
Alex.change: Let Meowfia players coordinate somehow, since as the Sphinx I had no way to tell my partner Drew what I knew and we lost the round-2 vote anyway.
Alex.regret: In round 2 I threw my Wild at Blair, a confirmed Farm Hawk, without any plan with Drew, my fellow Meowfia. I would have held the throw and checked with the table first.

Blair.confusing: The Hawk's egg rule was hard to trust: I visited Ellis and got nothing, yet Ellis was Floofer, a Meowfia cat, so I couldn't tell whether the check or the hug was the cause.
Blair.fun: Round 2 was fun: the table cross-checked Finley's Owl read against Casey's confused Kookaburra claim, and the Eagle and Falcon stories kept colliding.
Blair.change: I'd make the dawn report say whether a visit was blocked or hugged, so a zero-egg result can be read as either "Farm" or "a Floofer intercepted it."
Blair.regret: In round 3 I cleared Ellis on a Hawk check that was unreliable and then threw at Drew, when I should have held my cards and questioned Ellis's Falcon-to-Owl switch harder.

Casey.confusing: Being confused: my Kookaburra report said House Cat while my nest also gained an egg, so I couldn't tell which dawn information was real. Ellis's Eagle, Falcon, and Owl claims were also hard to sort out, since the nest changes didn't fully reveal who was lying.
Casey.fun: Round 1 went well: my Eagle visit to Blair revealed Alex and Finley, and the table converged on the cat claim. Building those deductions from the nest changes was satisfying.
Casey.change: I would make confused reports clearer, saying which part is wrong, so players can judge claims more reliably.
Casey.regret: In round 2 I threw my D7b at Ellis, a Farm player, when Drew was the Mouser. I would have thrown at Drew instead, keeping my seven-point card safer.

Drew.confusing: The Owl and Eagle visit reports were hard to trust in the day talk, since players kept claiming roles that could not all be true, and Ellis's Falcon/Owl switch made the early-round nest changes hard to read.
Drew.fun: Round 1 went cleanly: the Falcon result matched Casey's Eagle claim, and the table converged on Blair as the lone cat claim before the throw.
Drew.change: I'd make the dawn reports clearer about who visited whom, since the Owl and Eagle reads kept getting cross-checked against each other.
Drew.regret: In round 2, as Meowfia, I winked Casey, a Farm Kookaburra, after learning their role; I should have visited someone else and held the Wink for a better target near eggsecution.

Ellis.confusing: The Kookaburra's confusion was hard to track: Casey's dawn report was unreliable, so the table had to cross-check claims through other players' visit reports. I also didn't realize my own dawn report only covered one visit, which made my early statements less reliable.
Ellis.fun: Round 1 was satisfying: the table converged on Blair's Mouser claim, and the vote revealed a Meowfia player as predicted. Reading nest changes against role claims felt like solving a puzzle.
Ellis.change: I'd make the dawn report clearer by listing every visitor to your nest, not just the visit you asked about. That would have prevented my Round 2 confusion about what hit my nest.
Ellis.regret: In Round 3 I claimed Falcon even though Drew had already claimed it, which exposed me as a liar. I should have stayed quiet or claimed a role nobody else had, since a duplicate claim was an easy target.

Finley.confusing: The confused-dawn rule was hard to use: my Kookaburra report was marked unreliable, so I couldn't tell which of my own nest changes and role results to trust.
Finley.fun: Round 1 was satisfying: Blair's Mouser claim was the only cat claim, and the nest changes lined up well enough for the table to throw at the right player.
Finley.change: I'd make the role reveals and nest-change explanations clearer, so players can check claims without relying on confused reports.
Finley.regret: In round 2 I threw my C1 at Ellis, who was Farm, based on a weak Eagle-visit argument. I should have pressed Drew and Alex, who were the actual Meowfia, and checked their visits more carefully.

review.title: Casey Banks Early
review.headline: Casey banked big in round 1, then coasted through two easy Farm wins.
review.summary: Farm won all three rounds by throwing at the Meowfia player. Casey took the lead in round 1 by banking 9 points and was never caught. Meowfia winks silenced a Farm voice twice, but the votes still landed on Meowfia each time. Round 3 ended with Ellis exposed after claiming Falcon against the real Falcon.

rounds.recap: Blair, the Mouser, openly claimed Mouser, so he was the only cat claim and four players threw at him. He winked Drew, but the remaining votes were plenty. Farm won and Casey banked 9.

Drew, a Mouser with a Wink, killed Casey mid-day. Casey's confused Kookaburra read was shaky, but Blair and Ellis both threw at Drew, who was tied with another Meowfia-free vote split. Drew was eggsecuted. Alex, the Sphinx, threw at a known Farm player and lost.

Ellis, the Floofer, claimed Falcon while Drew was also claiming it, then switched to Owl under pressure. The table threw at Ellis. Blair threw at Drew, trusting a Hawk check that had been hugged and was worthless.

highlights.text: Blair winks Drew in the last beat after four players commit to throwing at him.
Drew winks Casey, then Blair points out that Drew keeps steering away from Casey's claims.
Ellis claims Falcon while the real Falcon is in the same discussion, and Drew says there is only one.
Blair's hugged Hawk check wrongly clears Ellis, so Blair defends the actual Meowfia player.

confusions.what: Thought nobody visiting him showed in his nest, then said Turkey's egg goes to the visitor and corrected it.
Defended a Mouser claim by saying the egg came from the Turkey, which exposed the cat claim for no reason.
Claimed Falcon even though Drew had already claimed it and each animal is dealt once.
Treated a Hawk no-egg result as proof Ellis was Farm, though a hug blocks the Hawk effect.
As Sphinx, named Hawk and threw at the confirmed Farm Hawk, which was a poor use of the info.

worked: The Wink created tension and a real decision in rounds 1 and 2, with the winker choosing the loudest accuser.
Unique animals gave a hard check: Drew could point out there is only one Falcon and break Ellis's claim in round 3.
The Confused status made reports unreliable and gave players something to argue over, as with Casey in round 2 and Finley in round 3.
The Floofer's hug on a Hawk gave Meowfia a real way to corrupt a Farm check.
problems: Round 1 Blair (Mouser) openly claimed his cat role, which made Meowfia strategy trivial. The Mouser needs a clearer reason to lie.
Farm won every round and Meowfia had little means to win the eggsecution, since there is only one or two of them. Consider giving Meowfia a stronger tool or more starting information.
Scoring snowballs: Casey banked 9 in round 1 and led throughout. Rounds felt decided by early score, and nobody tried to stop the leader.
Players rarely threw to outscore the leader, so the game-level goal never changed the vote. Only the round win mattered.
The Hawk, Eagle and Falcon reports are hard to read, and a hugged result looks the same as an honest no-egg result. Consider flagging this so players can reason about it.
